Money Stuff: Pre-IPO Perpetual Futures Swap ETF
items.summary: Money Stuff MANGOS, prime, longshots, buffet. MANGOS What is the best way to get economic exposure to Anthropic stock right now? There are bad answers ( expensive SPVs , fake SPVs ). Here are two arguably good answers: Just own Anthropic stock. Own perpetual futures on Anthropic stock on Hyperliquid. The first answer is pretty self-explanatory. Anthropic has stock, and people own it, and owning it gives you economic exposure to Anthropic stock. There are problems. Not just anyone can own Anthropic stock. It is a private company, and its shares do not trade on an exchange. You more or less need to get the stock from Anthropic , so this approach requires you to be an employee or a venture capital investor in one of its funding rounds or an effective altruist hedge fund manager . For most of us, that rules out this approach entirely. But there is another problem, even if you can get the stock. The other problem is that Anthropic stock is fairly illiquid. [1] You can’t easily sell it, until it goes public. Owning the stock gives you economic exposure to the stock, but you don’t get to decide how long you keep that exposure. And you don’t really know its price . So you do have economic exposure to the stock — if it goes up, your stock is worth more — but you don’t necessarily know how much. The second answer is weirder. Hyperliquid Labs runs a leading platform for trading perpetual futures contracts. Traditionally perpetual futures are a crypto thing, a way to make levered bets on cryptocurrencies, they have expanded into stocks and commodities. Kalshi launched an S&P 500 futures contract and is working on perpetual futures for individual stocks. Perpetual futures contracts are basically bets on prices: One person goes long, one person goes short, the short pays the long if the stock goes up, and the long pays the short if it goes down. A perpetual futures contract on an individual public stock is just a levered bet on that stock, and by arbitrage it will closely track the price of the underlying stock. If SpaceX stock trades at $167.60, and SpaceX perpetual futures trade at $165, arbitrageurs will buy the futures and sell the stock until the prices are in line, etc. [2] But perpetual futures on private stock have no arbitrage mechanism to make the price correct. If Anthropic perpetual futures trade at $120, while Anthropic’s stock is at $100, arbitrageurs cannot sell the futures and buy the stock until the prices converge: They can sell the futures, but they can’t buy the stock. [3] Also, how do you even know that “Anthropic’s stock is at $100”? Anthropic doesn’t trade liquidly or publicly, so you don’t know its price from minute to minute, the way you know the price of the futures. items.title: Money Stuff: ESG Gets More Illegal
items.summary: Is ESG illegal? US securities laws have rules restricting activist shareholders. The main ones are: If you acquire more than 5% of a company’s stock, and you plan on “ changing or influencing the control ” of the company, you have to promptly file a disclosure on Schedule 13D setting out your plans, your source of funds, etc. If you are a passive investor without any interest in changing or influencing control of the company, you can file a shorter, less detailed Schedule 13G . So if you are an activist hedge fund looking to run a proxy fight, and you go over 5%, you have to file a 13D; if you’re a normal mutual fund, you probably file a 13G. The point of the 13D is to alert the company, and its shareholders, to the fact that an activist is involved in its stock. If you team up with another investor — “when two or more persons act as a partnership, limited partnership, syndicate, or other group for the purpose of acquiring, holding, or disposing of securities of an issuer” — you are considered to be part of a “ group .” If you’re in a group, your shares are added together for securities-law purposes: If you own 3% of the company’s stock, and I own 3% of the company’s stock, and we agree to do an activist campaign together, then we form a group that owns 6% of the stock. So we need to file a joint Schedule 13D, disclosing that we are a group and own 6% of the shares. If you go over 10% of a company’s stock, you are restricted from trading the stock: If you buy stock and quickly sell it at a profit, you might have to give up those profits. (These are the “Section 16 short-swing profit rules .”) If your group goes over 10% of the stock, everyone in the group is subject to short-swing profit rules . This stuff is pretty vague. What does it mean to “change or influence the control” of a company? There are some obvious cases: If you are an activist hedge fund planning to run a proxy fight to replace the board of directors, or a potential buyer planning to launch a hostile takeover offer , you clearly want to change or influence the control of the company and you have to file a 13D. But if you are a regular old mutual fund that would never launch a proxy fight, you still might want to occasionally meet with the managers of the companies whose stock you own. In those meetings, you might ask questions and suggest ideas; you might say “hey I think you should expand the widget business and cut back on the sprockets,” or “man I did not like your last ad campaign,” or “what are you doing about climate change?” Are those efforts to “change or influence the control” of the company? Historically the answer has mostly been no; historically, everyone has assumed that 13D is for classic activists (who wage proxy fights), and that mutual funds can use 13G while still...

items.title: Money Stuff: Mergers and Acqui-hires
items.summary: Reverse acqui-hire In recent years, the US technology industry invented a new kind of mergers-and-acquisitions transaction. Traditionally there were two main sorts of M&A transaction: The acquirer buys the target company , in a merger or stock purchase; the shareholders of the target company get something (cash, acquirer stock) in exchange for their shares of the target, and the acquirer ends up owning the target corporate entity. The acquirer buys the assets of the company, in an asset purchase; the target company gets something (cash, acquirer stock) in exchange for its business. If the target is selling all of its assets, it will be left as an empty shell, and will probably distribute the cash or stock to its shareholders and liquidate. These are both pretty normal transactions, and many rules are set up to treat them similarly. So, for instance, Delaware corporate law requires a shareholder vote for a merger , or for a sale of “all or substantially all” of a company’s assets. US antitrust law requires a “Hart-Scott-Rodino premerger notification report” — where the acquirer tells antitrust regulators about the deal and gives them the opportunity to object — for any acquisition of more than $133.9 million worth of stock or assets. You might get different accounting or tax treatment for different deal structures, but many of the big-picture effects are the same however you structure the deal. The antitrust part is important. The big tech companies are very big, there is a lot of political and regulatory worry that they are monopolists, and there is at least some winner-takes-all flavor to the AI race. Meta or Alphabet or Nvidia might really want to do a $20 billion AI acquisition here or there, but that might be risky from an antitrust perspective. So they’re in the market for ways to do acquisitions without, technically, doing acquisitions. Many early-stage artificial intelligence startups consist mostly of (1) people and (2) ideas. The startup has some AI researchers, and they’ve come up with some model or harness or chip design or robot or whatever, and it’s pretty promising. But the startup doesn’t have, like, a giant portfolio of data-center real estate, or a robot assembly line, or a bunch of customer contracts. If a big tech company wants to acquire a startup like that, it could buy it in a merger, or buy all of its assets. But the new structure is: The acquirer hires the target’s employees, or most of them, or at least the people who are critical to its valuable ideas. The acquirer gets a waiver, from the target’s board of directors, allowing it to do all that hiring. items.title: Money Stuff: AI Agents Will Pay Attention
items.summary: Attention is all you need My little financials dispersion trade [1] is: Some retail-facing financial businesses make their money from customers who pay too little attention. Some retail-facing financial businesses make their money from customers who pay too much attention. Agentic artificial intelligence will tend to help customers pay more attention, which is bad or good for business, respectively. We’ve talked about both legs of this a few times recently. Recent worries about “ agentic bank runs ” reflect the fact that banks make a lot of their money from depositor inattention: When interest rates go up, bank customers mostly don’t move their money, because it would be a pain, so banks can pay below-market interest rates on their deposits. You could have similar worries about life insurance, or annuities, or mortgages : Lots of financial products are built (and priced) based on assumptions about customer inattention. AI agents, the theory goes, have unlimited attention and energy, and will tirelessly move money around to extract the last basis point from banks. (Here is a prescient 2019 law review article by Rory Van Loo on “ Digital Market Perfection ,” laying out this worry.) On the other hand, some retail brokerages are absolutely falling over themselves to get customers to adopt AI agents. Why? Because, simplistically, in modern US market structure, retail trades are profitable for brokerages. (Strictly: Retail trades are profitable for market makers who take the other side of those trades, and market makers pay brokerages to take the other side of their customers’ trades.) More retail trades mean more profits. But the customers have day jobs and family commitments and need to sleep, so they can only do so many trades per day. AI agents, the theory goes, have unlimited attention and energy and don’t sleep, so they will do many more trades. They will tirelessly move money around to pay the last basis point to market makers. Retail brokerages are actually an interesting case because, schematically, they make money in two ways: from trades (receiving payment for order flow from market makers), and from idle cash balances (investing customers’ cash, earning interest, and paying the customers a below-market portion of that interest). Trade revenue is increasing with attention, so agentic AI is probably good news for brokers on that front. Cash-balance revenue is decreasing with attention, so agentic AI is probably bad news for brokers on that front. I’ve also idly speculated about agentic sports gambling , which would be just pure windfall for sportsbooks and prediction markets. Today’s Wall Street Journal has articles about both legs of this trade. First: “ Lazy Customers Are Great for Banks. Could AI Change that? ” AI assistants may soon run your...

items.title: Money Stuff: Opening Private Markets to the Public
items.summary: Private markets are the new public markets: Performance fees A simple model is: Regular retail investors pay index fund managers fees of approximately 0.03% of assets. Sophisticated institutional investors pay hedge fund and private equity fund managers fees of approximately 2% of assets and 20% of returns, or sometimes much more. One possibility is that the retail investors are getting a much, much better deal. Another possibility is that the institutional investors are getting much, much better investment managers. Probably there is some truth to both theories. Of course this is a gross oversimplification. Institutional investors mostly don’t really pay 2-and-20 fees on their entire portfolios. Many of them put most of their money into regular stock index funds that charge very low fees, and some of their money into “alternatives” — hedge funds, private equity, venture capital — that charge high fees. But retail investors mostly don’t have any 2-and-20 investments at all. There are a lot of reasons for this difference, but one pretty simple one is that US securities rules generally don’t let retail investors pay 2-and-20 fees. US law generally prohibits registered fund managers from charging performance fees, that is, fees calculated as a percentage of returns. There are exceptions for fund managers whose clients are all “ qualified clients ,” meaning that they have net worth of at least $2.7 million or at least $1.4 million of assets under management at the fund company. [1] So a hedge fund that takes money only in large chunks from institutional investors and rich people can charge 20% of gains, but a mutual fund that takes money in $1,000 increments from anyone mostly can’t. Here is an intuitive story you might tell about the effects of this rule: If you’re very good at picking the stocks that will go up, you would rather do it for institutional investors in a hedge fund or private equity fund [2] (and get a cut of your winnings) than for retail investors in a mutual fund (and not get a cut). Over time, the best investors will work at hedge funds and private equity funds and the, uh, second-best will work at mutual funds. The hedge funds and private equity funds will outperform the market, while the mutual funds won’t. People will notice, and tell retail investors: “Hey, the mutual funds that you buy don’t outperform the market, but they charge like 1% management fees. You could just buy the whole market in an index fund, get similar or better performance, and pay much lower fees.” Eventually retail money will all migrate out of actively managed mutual funds that charge 1% fees and into index funds that charge like 0.03% fees. I came across some beautiful chanterelles at Uwajimaya while filming our Japanese Pantry Guide the other day, and while I normally make this pasta dish with much less expensive mushrooms, I love chanterelles enough that I couldn't resist. The good news is that the specific mushroom really isn't important here. Button or cremini mushrooms work great. So do shiitake, portobello, hen of the woods, oyster mushrooms, or virtually any mixture you can find at the grocery store or farmers market. The important part is giving the mushrooms enough heat and time to actually brown them before you start building the sauce. This is one of those pastas where the sauce doesn't really exist until the very end. You start by browning the mushrooms hard in olive oil (I like to throw in a thyme or rosemary sprig while the mushrooms sauté and fish it out later), then add a little onion or shallot and garlic. Kenji López-Alt Sep 11, 2026 View in app View in app Rich, juicy yellowtail collars grilled until crisp and charred, then lacquered with a glossy teriyaki glaze. Hamachi is a type of jack fish commonly sold as yellowtail (not to be confused with yellowfin tuna). The collar is the meat surrounding the neck and jowl of the fish—basically its fatty cheeks. I think of it as the guanciale of the fish: exceptionally rich, juicy, a little gelatinous, and very difficult to overcook. That last quality makes hamachi collar particularly well-suited to the grill. As it cooks, its abundant fat and connective tissue soften while the skin and exposed surfaces crisp and char. Unless things go catastrophically wrong, you only need to worry about properly charring the outside and the inside will take care of itself. The only real trick is dealing with its shape. A fish collar is curved and irregular, so it won't sit politely flat against the grill grate.
